title: Swap voltage-amplitude sensing for time-to-digital bitline sensing
idea: Substitute the voltage-amplitude latch with a time-domain sensor: the shared bitline charge sets the bias of a current-starved delay cell, and one 8-way time-to-digital arbiter shared by 8 bitline pairs decides which edge arrives first. Signal margin becomes picoseconds of delay instead of millivolts on a latch.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): pitch-matched latches shrink about 4x because the TDC sits off-pitch and is shared; tolerates 30-40% lower bitline swing, easing the Cs charge wall (fact 1).

title: Image-sensor ramp comparators replace per-bitline DRAM latch sense amps
idea: Substitute per-bitline cross-coupled latches with the column-parallel single-slope ramp comparator borrowed from CMOS image sensors. The bitlines act as analog sample-and-hold nodes, one comparator plus counter serially digitizes 16 bitlines against a global ramp, and a burst write driver then restores the row.
why: Periphery area: SA count drops 16x, cutting sense strip area by about 60%; slower random access suits streaming AI weight memory where bandwidth matters more than latency.

title: Merchant-foundry periphery wafers bonded to array-only DRAM wafers
idea: Substitute DRAM-process periphery with periphery made on depreciated 28/22 nm merchant-foundry logic lines and wafer-bonded to array-only wafers. DRAM fabs then spend all their EUV and DRAM-specific tool time on cell arrays, and periphery is bought by the wafer.
why: Capital intensity and capacity: with periphery at ~49% of die, array-only wafers yield ~1.8x more bits per DRAM-fab wafer start; idle mature-node US foundry capacity becomes DRAM supply.

title: Wavelength-coded optical row decoding with microring drop filters
idea: Substitute the electrical row decoder tree with wavelength selection: an on-die SiN waveguide carries one of N laser lines, a microring drop filter tuned to each row group routes it to a photodiode, and the photodiode triggers that group's local wordline driver. The address is the wavelength.
why: Periphery area and energy: removes multi-stage NAND decode trees and long address buses (~8-10% of die) and makes decode energy nearly independent of array size.

title: Self-timed sense completion replaces worst-case DRAM timing margins
idea: Substitute fixed worst-case timing (tRCD/tRAS guard bands) with asynchronous completion detection. Each sense latch drives dual-rail outputs, and a C-element tree over a mat raises 'row sensed' as soon as the slowest latch has actually resolved, so column access starts at the real finish time.
why: Latency and bandwidth: typical rows resolve 25-35% faster than the worst corner, recovering tRCD time and part of the 10-20% bandwidth lost to refresh (fact 3).

title: Resonant LC energy recovery for bitline precharge and restore
idea: Substitute dissipative CMOS precharge and restore with adiabatic swing: banks of bitlines are switched onto an in-package inductor so their charge rings sinusoidally between two bank groups instead of being dumped to ground and recharged from VDD.
why: Energy per bit (fact 10): bitline CV^2 dominates activate energy, and resonant recovery of 50-70% of that charge cuts activate/restore energy about 2x without lowering VARY.

title: Coincident row-and-column-group selection borrowed from core memory
idea: Substitute single-wordline activation with core-memory coincident selection: the access transistor is dual-gated, with the top gate on the row line and a buried back gate on a column-group line, and it conducts only when both are high. Only a 512-bit segment of the row opens.
why: Destructive-read overfetch (fact 8): activated bits drop from ~8K to 512, cutting energy per useful bit up to ~16x on random access, and less charge disturbance also eases row hammer.

title: Token-passing shift-chain wordline sequencer for streaming weight memory
idea: Substitute the random-access row decoder with a one-flop-per-wordline token chain that steps to the next row on each activate, plus a coarse jump decoder every 64 rows. This targets AI weight and KV streaming, where row order is known.
why: Periphery area: row decode logic shrinks ~60% and wordline select energy drops to one flop toggle; fits HBM-class AI memory, where streaming dominates.

title: Analog leaky-capacitor activation integrator replaces row-hammer counter tables
idea: Substitute digital SRAM activation-counter tables with a per-row analog integrator: each activate dumps a fixed charge packet onto a small leaky capacitor in the wordline driver, and when a Schmitt detector trips, the neighbors are refreshed. The leak rate itself sets the time window.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): exact per-row tracking at ~2 transistors + 1 cap per row instead of large CAM/SRAM trackers, which fail at 1k-activation thresholds.

title: Soft-decision dual-time latch sampling feeds on-die LDPC
idea: Substitute the hard binary sense decision with soft information: each latch output is sampled at an early and a late strobe, and disagreement flags a low-confidence bit. An on-die soft-decision LDPC over 512-bit column words then corrects them.
why: Charge wall and refresh (facts 1, 3): tolerating ~2x lower signal margin allows Cs ~3 fF instead of 5 fF, or 2-4x longer refresh intervals.

title: Dithered minimum-size comparator triplets replace large matched sense pairs
idea: Substitute one large, carefully matched sense pair with three minimum-size comparators per bitline pair, each fed an independent small dither offset, followed by a 3-input majority gate before the restore latch fires. Random offsets average instead of being sized away.
why: Periphery area: matching-driven transistor sizing is the main SA area cost; three minimum devices plus majority cost ~40% less area at equal bit-error rate.

title: Liquid-nitrogen DRAM with double-length copper bitlines
idea: Substitute room-temperature operation with 77 K operation: copper resistivity falls ~7x and junction/GIDL leakage effectively disappears, so bitlines can run 1024 cells instead of 512 and refresh is dropped for datacenter racks with LN2 loops.
why: Periphery area and refresh (facts 3, 7): halving the SA count saves ~15% of die, and refresh energy and bandwidth loss go to ~0.

title: Spare cell-capacitor pillars serve as charge-pump flying capacitors
idea: Substitute planar MOS capacitors in the VPP/VBB charge pumps with blocks of ordinary high-aspect-ratio array capacitor pillars, placed in dummy mats and wired in parallel as flying and reservoir capacitors.
why: Periphery area: array caps store ~50-100x more charge per um^2 than gate-oxide caps, shrinking pump area ~80% (pumps are several % of die) with zero new process steps.

title: MTJ-shadowed sense latches give a nonvolatile row buffer
idea: Substitute the purely volatile sense latch with a latch shadowed by a pair of MTJs written on precharge. Periphery can then be hard power-gated between bursts, and open rows reload from the MTJs in nanoseconds without reactivating the array.
why: Idle energy: periphery leakage dominates idle power at advanced nodes; power-gating plus instant row-buffer recall cuts idle power by ~30-50% and avoids re-activate energy.

title: Controller-side remap tables replace on-die fuse redundancy
idea: Substitute on-die laser/e-fuse banks and redundancy address comparators with a per-device bad-row/bad-column table held by the memory controller (like an SSD FTL), filled at test and refreshed during field scrubbing.
why: Periphery area and yield: removes ~3-5% of die area for fuses and compare logic, and finer-grained repair raises yield on immature nodes.

title: Deliberately weakened canary cells trigger refresh on physical decay
idea: Substitute timer-driven refresh with physical sensing: each mat carries replica canary cells with ~30% smaller Cs and a longer-leakage access device, read by a dedicated sense amp. A mat refreshes only when its canary flips, so the interval follows the real temperature and leakage.
why: Refresh (fact 3): at typical datacenter temperatures retention is far above the 32/64 ms worst case, so refresh energy and bandwidth loss drop 50-80%.

title: Pulsed back-plate biasing replaces 3 V thick-oxide wordline drivers
idea: Substitute the boosted ~3 V wordline with a buried back plate under each mat that is pulsed during access to lower the access-transistor Vt and held negative during retention. Wordlines then swing only ~1.2 V through thin-oxide drivers.
why: Voltage floor and periphery area (facts 7, 10): drivers shrink ~3x, charge-pump load drops sharply, and wordline CV^2 falls ~6x.

title: Top-metal inductive coils over arrays replace HBM TSVs
idea: Substitute through-silicon vias with near-field inductive coil pairs drawn in top metal directly above the cell arrays, which use no silicon area. Stacked dies talk through face-to-back magnetic coupling.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): removes TSV keep-out zones and TSV-related yield loss (20-30%), cutting area per bit and stacking cost.

title: Capacitor-DAC successive approximation sense for two-bit cells
idea: Substitute the single-threshold latch with a two-step successive-approximation comparison: switched trim capacitors on the reference bitline act as a capacitive DAC that steps the reference to resolve four stored charge levels, so each cell holds 2 bits.
why: Density and cost per bit: ~2x bits per cell area if sense resolution reaches ~25 mV steps, which is helped by soft-decision ECC.

title: Steep-slope tunnel-FET sense amps enable 0.5 V array voltage
idea: Substitute MOSFET sense pairs with heterojunction tunnel FETs (~30 mV/dec) used only in the latch, where low drive current matters less, so the array voltage drops from ~1 V to ~0.5 V while the latch still regenerates.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): array CV^2 falls ~4x; leakage at low VARY also falls.

title: Self-referenced two-pulse sensing eliminates reference bitlines
idea: Substitute the external reference (dummy cell or VDD/2 twin bitline) with the cell itself: read once, inject a known small charge step into the same cell, read again, and let the sign of the difference give the data. This is the self-reference trick from MRAM applied to DRAM.
why: Density: makes open-bitline, near-4F^2 layouts tolerable without reference-mismatch errors, gaining ~1.3-1.5x cell density.

title: Keyed Feistel scrambler in decoder randomizes physical row adjacency
idea: Substitute the fixed logical-to-physical row map with a tiny keyed Feistel permutation in the row predecoder, re-keyed each refresh epoch with background migration, so attackers cannot know which physical rows neighbor their aggressors.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): defeats targeted many-sided hammering at a few hundred gates per bank instead of large counter tables.

title: Column-periphery zero-skip compression replaces raw data serialization
idea: Substitute raw serialization of the row buffer with zero-run and base-delta compression units in the column periphery that send only non-zero bytes plus a bitmask over the interface. This exploits sparse AI activations and KV caches.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): 1.5-3x fewer bits on the wire for sparse tensors, cutting I/O energy and raising effective bandwidth and capacity.

title: Sputtered IGZO thin-film decoders stacked above the cell array
idea: Substitute crystalline-silicon row decoders with sputtered IGZO TFT decoders built at <=350 C on top of the array (ALD HfO2 gate, Mo source/drain). A university nanofab can demonstrate a 64-row decoder over a MIM-cap test array with i-line lithography.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): moving decode above the array reclaims ~10-15% of die; low-temperature BEOL process, no EUV.

title: Ferroelectric HZO polarization stores per-amp offset trim
idea: Substitute large matched sense transistors with minimum-size FeFETs whose ALD HZO gate polarization is partially switched at test to null each amp's offset, so the trim is stored as analog polarization. HZO ALD, TiN sputter and RTA are standard nanofab tools.
why: Periphery area: offset-limited SA area shrinks ~3-5x once mismatch is trimmed instead of sized away.

title: Thin-film AlN piezoelectric transformer replaces wordline charge pumps
idea: Substitute switched-capacitor VPP charge pumps with a released thin-film AlN contour-mode piezoelectric transformer that steps 1.1 V to ~3 V at resonance. AlN sputtering, XeF2 release and e-beam electrodes are university-fab processes.
why: Periphery energy and area: piezo transformers can reach >80% conversion efficiency against ~30-50% for multi-stage pumps, cutting wordline supply energy ~2x.

title: Nanoelectromechanical relay decoders with zero off-state leakage
idea: Substitute CMOS decoder and wordline-isolation transistors with electrostatically actuated TiN or poly-Si NEM relays (sacrificial oxide release, e-beam gaps ~50 nm). Relays have truly zero off-current and abrupt switching.
why: Idle energy: removes decoder/driver subthreshold leakage, which dominates standby, and abrupt switching allows low-voltage decode logic.

title: Series negative-capacitance HZO capacitor as passive bitline amplifier
idea: Substitute part of the transistor gain with a passive voltage step-up: a doped-HZO capacitor biased in its negative-capacitance region sits in series between the bitline and the latch input, so the transient voltage at the latch is amplified ~2-5x. It is buildable with ALD and e-beam in a university fab.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): if verified, the same latch resolves with ~2x less cell charge, relaxing capacitor aspect ratio.

title: Shadow-evaporated single-electron transistor electrometers sense cryo-DRAM bits
idea: Substitute the CMOS sense amp with an Al/AlOx single-electron transistor (double-angle shadow evaporation, e-beam resist bridge) whose island couples to the bitline, reading sub-attofarad charge for 4 K memory beside quantum processors.
why: Charge wall: cell capacitance could shrink ~100x for cryogenic memory, making a planar cell possible with no high-AR capacitor.

title: NbN nanocryotron sense amplifiers with superconducting niobium bitlines
idea: Substitute both the copper bitline and the CMOS latch with superconductors: zero-resistance Nb bitlines feed an e-beam-patterned NbN nanocryotron (nTron) whose choke switches the channel normal when the bitline current exceeds its threshold.
why: Energy per bit: superconducting sensing costs aJ per event and has no bitline RC, enabling multi-thousand-cell bitlines and ~10x fewer sense amps for cryogenic computing.

title: Geiger-mode avalanche junction as a digital charge-threshold detector
idea: Substitute the regenerative latch with an implanted silicon p-n junction biased just below avalanche (as in SPAD pixels) with a quench resistor: the bitline signal pushes it over breakdown or not, giving a full-swing digital output in ~100 ps. Implant, anneal and contact are basic nanofab steps.
why: Charge wall and SA area: avalanche gain of 10^5 or more resolves femtocoulomb signals in one compact junction plus resistor.

title: Randomly coded nanowire decoders mapped after fabrication
idea: Substitute lithographically exact decoders with an e-beam nanowire array whose gate oxide is randomly modulated (random doping or random dielectric patches). After fabrication a tester discovers each wire's address code and stores the map.
why: Litho and capital (fact 4): decoders can sit at sub-litho pitch without alignment, tolerating defects through discovery instead of precision.

title: CCD charge shifting replaces bitlines for column readout
idea: Substitute the bitline with a polysilicon charge-coupled column: stored charge packets are clocked down the column like a CCD imager to a single floating-diffusion sense node at the column end. This revives 1970s CCD memory for sequential AI streams with two-level poly in a university fab.
why: Periphery and charge wall: one SA per column instead of per bitline pair, and floating-diffusion gain lets small packets be sensed.

title: Thin-film Schottky diode-matrix passive row decoder
idea: Substitute transistor NAND decode trees with a 1950s-style diode-matrix decoder made of thin-film Pt/IGZO Schottky diodes at address-line crossings, so only the selected row line stays high. It needs two masks plus sputtering.
why: Periphery area: decode moves into a passive crossbar layer that can sit over the array, and the transistor count of decoders drops ~5x.

title: Goto-pair Esaki tunnel-diode latch as sense amplifier
idea: Substitute the cross-coupled inverter latch with a Goto pair: two series Esaki tunnel diodes whose negative differential resistance forms a bistable node that the bitline signal tips one way. Degenerately doped Si or uni-MBE InGaAs junctions are within university reach.
why: Speed and energy: NDR latching switches in ps at ~0.3 V, cutting sense energy and allowing lower array voltage (fact 10).

title: RF reflectometry reads bitlines through on-chip LC resonators
idea: Substitute DC charge-sharing readout with RF reflectometry, as used for qubit readout: each bitline is part of a spiral-inductor LC tank whose MOS-varactor tuning depends on the cell charge, and a frequency-multiplexed probe tone reads many bitlines on one line from phase shifts.
why: Periphery area: frequency multiplexing lets one RF readout chain serve dozens of bitlines, replacing pitch-matched latches.

title: Sputtered NbO2 Mott threshold switch as sense comparator
idea: Substitute the transistor comparator with a two-terminal NbO2 insulator-metal-transition device biased just below its threshold: bitline signal above the reference triggers abrupt (~ns) conduction that sets the restore driver. Reactive sputtering and e-beam pillars suffice.
why: Periphery area: a two-terminal device fits at bitline pitch in a via, shrinking sense strips ~2-3x.

title: Dopant-free undoped nanowire channels shrink sense-amp mismatch
idea: Substitute doped-channel sense transistors with undoped SOI nanowire gate-all-around devices whose Vt is set by gate work function (TiN/TaN), removing random dopant fluctuation. Oxidation thinning and e-beam patterning are university-standard.
why: Periphery area: sigma-Vt drops ~3x, so pitch-matched SA area shrinks up to ~5-9x (area scales with 1/sigma^2).

title: Two-terminal ovonic threshold switches replace bitline equalize transistors
idea: Substitute the three-transistor precharge/equalize block with sputtered GeSe-class ovonic threshold switches between bitline pairs and the precharge rail, fired by a short overdrive pulse.
why: Periphery area: equalizers sit at bitline pitch in vias rather than in active silicon, freeing ~10% of the sense strip.

title: Molybdenum replaces tungsten in wordline straps and contacts
idea: Substitute tungsten wordline straps and periphery contacts with barrier-thin ALD or sputtered molybdenum, which keeps lower resistivity at narrow widths, so each local wordline driver can serve ~2x more cells.
why: Scarce resources and periphery: removes dependence on China-dominated tungsten (~80%) in favor of US-mined Mo, and halves local wordline driver count.

title: Nanoimprint-patterned pitch-matched sense and decoder strips
idea: Substitute immersion/EUV exposures of the highly repetitive pitch-matched sense-amp and subword-driver strips with UV nanoimprint from an e-beam-written master. University nanofabs routinely run NIL for such periodic patterns.
why: Capital (fact 4): imprint tools cost ~1/20 of a scanner per layer, and periodic periphery is ideal imprint content.

title: Sacrificial-polymer air-gap bitlines raise sense transfer ratio
idea: Substitute oxide bitline spacers with vacuum: a sacrificial polymer between bitlines is thermally decomposed through a porous cap, lowering bitline capacitance. Spin-coat, cap and bake steps fit a university fab.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): Cbl drops ~30-40%, raising signal Cs/(Cs+Cbl) ~1.4x, so Cs can shrink or bitlines can lengthen with fewer sense amps.

title: Analog-voltage address bus with per-row window comparators
idea: Substitute the binary multi-wire address bus with two analog address lines (row-group and row-within-group voltages); each wordline driver carries a resistor-ladder window comparator that fires only when both voltages land in its window, which is coincidence decoding in the analog domain.
why: Periphery area: replaces ~16 address wires and NAND trees with 2 lines plus local comparators, simplifying routing in narrow sub-array gaps.

title: One-time ReRAM-programmed crossbar decoder routes around defects
idea: Substitute hard-wired decoders with a crossbar of HfOx ReRAM switches programmed once at test to connect each address code to any healthy physical row. Decoding and redundancy repair merge into one reconfigurable layer.
why: Yield and periphery: removes separate redundancy decoders and lets any spare row replace any failed row, raising yield on low-cost processes.

title: Laser-crystallized poly-Si repeaters amplify bitlines every 32 cells
idea: Substitute one long passive bitline feeding one end latch with a distributed bitline: excimer-laser-crystallized poly-Si TFT repeater stages every 32 cells regenerate the charge-shared signal locally, as display backplanes do.
why: Charge wall: each segment sees only 32 cells of bitline capacitance, giving ~8x higher signal per femtofarad and allowing much smaller Cs.

title: Open university interposer testbed decouples arrays from sensing logic
idea: Substitute captive DRAM-fab periphery development with an open platform: a university-built passive Si interposer with 2 um microbumps joins test cell arrays (MIM caps plus IGZO access devices) to FPGA or shuttle-ASIC sense logic, so any lab can iterate on sensing schemes in weeks.
why: US manufacturability and innovation speed: lowers the cost of experimenting with new sensing physics from fab-scale to ~$100k, broadening the US talent and IP base.
